title: Design of canals
summary: Kennedy and Lacey are the two silt theories, and the distinction that matters is that Kennedy ignores the channel WIDTH — so it needs an assumed B/D ratio and gives no unique section, while Lacey's regime equations give a unique section from discharge and silt factor alone. Beyond that, the reliable marks are the alignment types (a ridge canal irrigates both sides and crosses no drainage, a contour canal one side and crosses every drain), the reason for canal falls, and the balancing depth concept.

sections.heading: Classification and alignment of canals
sections.body:
**Classification by function:**

| Canal | Function |
|---|---|
| **Main canal** | Takes water from the headworks; **carries but does not usually irrigate** directly |
| **Branch canal** | Takes off from the main canal; also mainly a carrier |
| **Major distributary** | Takes off from a branch; irrigates through outlets |
| **Minor distributary** | Smaller; feeds watercourses |
| **Watercourse (field channel)** | The farmer's channel, from the outlet to the field |

**By other bases:**

| Basis | Types |
|---|---|
| Source | **Permanent** (from a perennial river or reservoir), **inundation** (flows only in flood season) |
| Function | Irrigation, **power**, navigation, feeder, carrier, **link** |
| Discharge | Main, branch, distributary, minor, watercourse |
| Alignment | **Ridge (watershed)**, **contour**, **side slope** |
| Lining | Lined or unlined |
| Boundary | **Alluvial** (silt-transporting, erodible) or **non-alluvial / rigid** (rock, lined) |

**The alluvial / non-alluvial distinction governs which design method applies**, and it is the first question to settle:

| Boundary | Design by |
|---|---|
| **Non-alluvial or LINED** | **Manning's or Chézy's equation** with a permissible velocity — the boundary does not move |
| **Alluvial, UNLINED** | **Kennedy's or Lacey's silt theory** — the channel must neither silt up nor scour |

**Alignment — the three types and their consequences:**

| Alignment | Runs along | Irrigates | Cross-drainage |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Ridge (watershed) canal** | The **ridge line** between two drainages | **BOTH sides**, by gravity | **NONE required** — it crosses no drainage |
| **Contour canal** | Roughly along a **contour**, across the slope | **ONE side only** (the downhill side) | **Crosses EVERY drainage** — many works needed |
| **Side slope canal** | **Down the slope**, parallel to the drainage | Both sides, but steeply | None, but needs many **falls** |

**The ridge canal is the ideal** and the reason is worth stating fully: running along the watershed, it has ground falling away on both sides, so it can **command land in both directions by gravity**, and since a ridge is by definition the divide between drainages, **no stream crosses it** — so no aqueducts, super-passages or siphons are needed. That combination makes it both the most productive and the cheapest alignment, and it is why the great canal systems of the Indo-Gangetic plain follow ridges.

**The contour canal is the usual case in hill country**, because there is no useful ridge to follow. It commands only the downhill side, and it must cross every stream coming down the slope — so it needs a **cross-drainage work at each one**, which is why hill canals are expensive per unit of area served. The Nepali hills are contour-canal country, and it explains why irrigation development there is costly.

**The side slope canal** runs down the slope and therefore has a bed slope much steeper than the canal needs, so it requires frequent **falls** to dissipate the excess. It crosses no drainage because it runs parallel to it.

**Alignment considerations** in practice: keep the canal on the **watershed** wherever possible; avoid **deep cutting and high filling** (both expensive and, in filling, prone to failure); avoid **unstable slopes, marshy ground and rocky reaches**; cross drainage at **right angles** where a crossing is unavoidable (shortest structure); avoid **villages, orchards and religious sites**; and keep the alignment **as short as possible** consistent with the above.

**The canal must also command its area**, which is the constraint easily overlooked: the **full supply level (FSL) must be above the highest field to be irrigated**, with allowance for the losses in the watercourse. A canal that is hydraulically perfect but 200 mm too low commands nothing.

sections.heading: Silt theories — Kennedy and Lacey
sections.body:
**The problem.** An unlined canal in alluvium has an erodible bed and carries silt. If the velocity is **too low** the silt **deposits** and the canal silts up; if **too high** the bed and banks **scour**. A stable canal must therefore run at a velocity that neither deposits nor scours — and the theories exist to find it.

**Kennedy's theory (1895)**, from observations on the Upper Bari Doab Canal:

> **Critical velocity V₀ = 0.55 m y^{0.64}**

where **y** is the **full supply depth** in metres and **m** the **critical velocity ratio** (CVR) accounting for silt grade:

| Silt grade | m |
|---|---|
| Very fine | 0.7 |
| Fine | 0.85 |
| **Standard** | **1.0** |
| Coarse | 1.1 – 1.2 |
| Very coarse | 1.3 |

Kennedy's reasoning was that the **silt is held in suspension by eddies rising from the BED**, so the sediment-carrying capacity depends on the **bed width**... and the depth. The velocity is then compared with Manning's or Kutter's equation to close the problem.

**Kennedy's fundamental limitation — the examinable point:**

> **Kennedy's theory takes NO ACCOUNT of the channel WIDTH.**

Since the critical velocity depends only on the depth, and Manning's equation involves the hydraulic radius, there are **two equations and three unknowns** (B, y, S). So the designer must **assume** either the **bed width to depth ratio (B/y)** or the **bed slope**, and the theory gives **no unique section** — different assumptions give different, equally "valid" answers. It also gives no way to determine the **slope** independently, which must be taken from experience or from a similar canal.

**Lacey's theory (1930)** addressed exactly that. Lacey argued that a channel in alluvium adjusts its **width, depth AND slope** until it reaches **regime** — a state in which it neither silts nor scours — and that all three can be predicted from the discharge and the silt grade.

**Lacey's regime equations:**

> **Silt factor f = 1.76 √m_r**   (m_r = mean particle size in mm)
> **Wetted perimeter P = 4.75 √Q**
> **Area A = 2.28 Q^{5/6} / f^{1/3}** (equivalently A = √(Q P /(something)); the standard forms vary)
> **Hydraulic radius R = 0.48 (Q/f)^{1/3}**
> **Velocity V = 0.4382 (Q f²)^{1/6}**
> **Slope S = f^{5/3} / (3340 Q^{1/6})**

The silt factor: **f = 1.0** corresponds to standard silt of mean size **0.323 mm**; a **larger f means coarser material**, hence a **steeper** regime slope.

**Kennedy versus Lacey — the comparison to hold:**

| | **Kennedy** | **Lacey** |
|---|---|---|
| Concept | A **critical velocity** for non-silting, non-scouring | A **regime** state of width, depth and slope together |
| Silt held up by | Eddies from the **bed** | Eddies from the **whole wetted perimeter** |
| Determines | Velocity only | **Width, depth, velocity AND slope** |
| Section obtained | **Not unique** — needs an assumed B/y | **Unique**, from Q and f |
| Slope | Must be **assumed** from experience | **Predicted** |
| Silt grade allowed for by | **CVR (m)** | **Silt factor (f)** |
| Character | Semi-empirical, simpler | More complete, more widely used |

**Lacey's advantage is that it closes the problem**, giving a unique answer without an arbitrary assumption. That is why Lacey's equations are the ones used in practice for alluvial canal design, and why a question asking which theory "gives a unique section" or "determines the slope" is asking for Lacey.

**Both theories have limits worth knowing**, because a question may ask when they do not apply: both are **empirical**, derived from specific canal systems in specific alluvium, and neither accounts for the **actual sediment load** entering the canal, for **bed forms**, or for **non-uniform sediment**. They apply to **alluvial** channels only — a lined or rock-cut canal is designed by Manning with a permissible velocity, and applying Lacey to it is a category error.

**Modern practice** uses **tractive force (Shields) theory** for a more rational treatment: the design condition is that the **shear stress on the bed must not exceed the critical value** to move the particle size present:

> **τ₀ = γ R S ≤ τ_critical**

This has the merit of being based on the actual physics of particle movement rather than on regional observation, and it handles lined, unlined and armoured channels within one framework.

sections.heading: Canal cross-section and lining
sections.body:
**The trapezoidal section is standard**, because it is the shape an earth channel naturally takes and the most economical to excavate.

**Side slopes** depend on the soil and on whether the canal is in cutting or filling:

| Soil | Cutting | Filling |
|---|---|---|
| Rock | 0.25:1 to vertical | — |
| Stiff clay, gravel | **1:1** | 1.5:1 |
| **Ordinary earth** | **1:1 to 1.5:1** | **1.5:1 to 2:1** |
| Sandy soil | 2:1 | 2:1 to 3:1 |

**Filling always takes flatter slopes than cutting** in the same soil, because a fill is a made embankment of remoulded, less consolidated material and must be stable against both its own weight and the seepage through it.

**Free board** — the height of the bank above the full supply level:

| Discharge | Free board |
|---|---|
| Up to 0.75 m³/s | **0.30 m** |
| 0.75 – 1.5 | 0.45 m |
| 1.5 – 85 | 0.60 m |
| **Over 85 m³/s** | **0.75 m** |

**Its purpose is not hydraulic capacity** but a margin of safety: it contains **wave action**, **surges from gate operation**, the **uncertainty of the design flow**, and settlement of the bank. Treating free board as spare capacity — and running the canal into it — removes exactly the margin it exists to provide.

**Berms** are horizontal shelves left on the slope, and they serve several purposes: they **increase the stability** of a deep cutting, provide a **service road**, catch material sliding from above, and — as silt deposits on them over time — the canal naturally **approaches its regime section**.

**Balancing depth** is the economic optimum in a canal that is part in cutting and part in filling:

> **The BALANCING DEPTH is the cutting depth at which the excavated volume exactly equals the volume required for the embankment.**

At that depth there is **no borrow pit and no spoil disposal** — the excavation supplies exactly the fill needed, and both the cost of importing fill and the cost of removing surplus vanish. It is found by equating the areas of cut and fill in the cross-section, and it is a standard numerical question.

**Canal lining** — the case for and against:

| Benefit | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Reduces seepage** | 60–80% of seepage eliminated; the primary benefit |
| **Prevents waterlogging** | Follows from the above |
| **Permits a higher velocity** | Hence a **smaller section** and less land |
| **Prevents weed growth** | Weeds increase roughness and reduce capacity |
| **Prevents erosion of bed and banks** | Stable section, lower maintenance |
| **Reduces maintenance cost** | No annual desilting or weed clearance |
| Safety against breaching | A lined bank is far less likely to fail |

Against which: **high capital cost**, difficulty of **repair** once cracked, difficulty of taking **outlets** through the lining, and the **loss of groundwater recharge** — which, as noted in the efficiency discussion, is not always a loss at all.

**Types of lining:**

| Lining | Character |
|---|---|
| **Cement concrete (cast in situ)** | **The best** — durable, smooth (n ≈ 0.014), impervious; most expensive |
| Precast concrete slabs | Quick, good quality control; joints are the weakness |
| **Shotcrete** | Thin, sprayed; good for repair and irregular surfaces |
| **Brick lining** | **Cheap where bricks are local**; common in the subcontinent; double layer with mortar |
| Stone / boulder lining | Where stone is abundant — much of Nepal |
| **Compacted earth / clay** | Cheapest; suitable where a clay blanket is available |
| **LDPE / geomembrane** | Very effective and cheap, but **must be covered** to protect from UV and damage |
| Asphalt / bituminous | Flexible; used in some large canals |

**The economic test for lining** is straightforward and worth stating, because it explains why canals are not universally lined:

> Lining is justified where the **annual value of the water saved (plus maintenance saved) exceeds the annualised cost of the lining**.

So lining pays where the **seepage rate is high** (sandy or fissured reaches), where **water is valuable** (scarce, or needed for an additional crop), and where **waterlogging** would otherwise damage land. It does not pay in a low-seepage clay reach with abundant water — which is why the correct practice is to **line the high-seepage reaches selectively**, identified by **ponding tests or inflow–outflow measurement**, rather than lining the whole length uniformly.

**Seepage loss measurement:**

| Method | How |
|---|---|
| **Ponding test** | Isolate a reach with bunds and measure the **fall in water level** over time — the most accurate |
| **Inflow–outflow method** | Measure discharge at two sections; the difference is the loss. Simple, but the difference is small relative to the measurement error |
| Seepage meter | Direct local measurement |
| Empirical formulae | Preliminary estimates |

**Canal falls** — the last element of the cross-section design, and the reason for them is worth stating precisely:

> A **canal fall** is provided where the **NATURAL GROUND SLOPE is STEEPER than the designed canal bed slope**.

Without falls, the canal would either run in progressively deeper cutting (uneconomical, and eventually it loses command) or, if it followed the ground, exceed its permissible non-scouring velocity. A fall drops the bed level abruptly and dissipates the excess energy in a controlled structure.

**Types of fall:**

| Fall | Character |
|---|---|
| **Ogee fall** | Smooth curved profile; no energy dissipation, so it needs downstream protection |
| **Rapid fall** | A long sloping glacis; used for large drops on a steep slope |
| **Stepped fall** | A series of steps; dissipates energy well |
| **Trapezoidal notch fall** | Maintains the **normal depth** upstream over a range of discharge |
| **Vertical drop (Sarda type)** | A vertical wall with a cistern below; **simple and widely used** |
| **Glacis fall (straight or parabolic)** | A **hydraulic jump forms on the glacis** — controlled, predictable energy dissipation; the modern choice |
| Well type (cylinder) fall | For a small discharge and a large drop |

**The glacis fall is preferred in modern practice** because the **hydraulic jump forms in a known position on the glacis**, where a concrete cistern can be provided to contain it — rather than occurring somewhere downstream in the earth channel, where it would scour.

**Falls are combined with other structures wherever possible** — with a **regulator**, a **bridge**, a **canal outlet** or a **metering flume** — because the excavation, foundation and approach works are then shared, and a single structure serves several purposes. That combination is a genuine economy and a standard design practice.

formulas.label: Kennedy's critical velocity
formulas.expression: V₀ = 0.55 m y^{0.64}     (m = critical velocity ratio, y = full supply depth)
formulas.note: Takes NO account of channel WIDTH, so it gives no unique section and cannot predict the slope.

formulas.label: Lacey's regime equations
formulas.note: Gives a UNIQUE section and predicts the slope — Lacey's advantage over Kennedy.

formulas.label: Lacey's silt factor
formulas.expression: f = 1.76 √m_r     (m_r = mean particle size in mm)
formulas.note: f = 1.0 for standard silt of 0.323 mm. A larger f (coarser material) gives a steeper regime slope.

formulas.label: Tractive force criterion
formulas.note: The rational modern approach — based on particle movement physics rather than regional observation.

formulas.label: Free board
formulas.expression: 0.30 m up to 0.75 m³/s ; 0.60 m for 1.5–85 m³/s ; 0.75 m above 85 m³/s
formulas.note: A safety margin for waves, surges and flow uncertainty — NOT spare hydraulic capacity.

formulas.label: Balancing depth
formulas.expression: The cutting depth at which excavated volume = embankment volume required
formulas.note: Eliminates both borrow and spoil disposal — the economic optimum for a part-cut, part-fill canal.

formulas.label: Canal fall — when required
formulas.expression: Where the natural GROUND slope is STEEPER than the designed canal BED slope
formulas.note: A glacis fall is preferred, because the hydraulic jump forms in a known position on the glacis.

formulas.label: Economic test for lining
formulas.expression: Line where the annual value of water and maintenance saved exceeds the annualised lining cost
formulas.note: So line the high-seepage reaches selectively, identified by ponding tests — not uniformly.
